Press Release:


Terror’s Tentacles
Four young Muslims were this week arrested amidst allegations of recruitment for the Islamic State and plans to target American and Jewish institutions in South Africa. Carte Blanche asks: how have international terror networks extended their tentacles into South Africa to recruit militant young adults for the cause?


Script:


Tentacles Of Terror
Script 15 July 2016

Voice
This is an example of an Islamic State of Iraq and Syria, or ISIS, propaganda video. Released on the Internet and often spread to loyal followers via a variety of social media platforms, the videos glorify war and violence, promise ISIS supporters a better life and often contain footage of the terrorist organization’s brutal trademark - beheadings too graphic to show on television.

Link Devi
ISIS uses social media to recruit on a scale we have never seen before – a scale which cannot be underestimated or ignored.

Sound Up Martin Ewi
The medium for these terrorist groups, it’s so vast, more vast than we’ve ever seen before, and that’s why the mass recruitment of these young people is so much that you know it’s a record, it’s unprecedented.

Voice
Martin Ewi is a senior researcher at the Institute for Security Studies who specializes in counter terrorism. He says social media platforms like Facebook and Twitter have made it very easy for especially young people to be exposed to terrorist ideologies.

Sound Up Martin
They are looking for a cause, they are looking for heroism.

Voice Over
Whatever the allure, ISIS has been extremely successful in recruiting foreign fighters to their cause. Of an estimated 31 000 fighters inside Syria and Iraq, nearly two thirds are foreigners.

Sound Up British Citizen
Know that if you fear death and that’s what prevents you, death will reach you anyway. But it will be more painful for you then those who get Shihada. Because the Shihada does not feel death, except like the sting of an insect.

Voice
Last week twin brothers Brandon-Lee and Tony-Lee Thulsie were arrested in Johannesburg by the Hawks. The 23 year olds were charged under the Protection of Constitutional Democracy against Terrorist and Related Activities Act. According to the provisional charge sheet, they were planning to cause explosions at a mission of the United States of America and Jewish Institutions in South Africa.

Sound Up Martin
I was very delighted first to hear of the arrests, coming just after the US terror alerts just last month of course which also came last year. So I see really a link between the two, even though the security officials have denied any links between the two.

Voice
Salomi Mckuur is Brandon and Tony Lee Thulsie’s sister. This is the first time a member of the family has spoken on television to the media since the brothers, dubbed the “terror twins” in the headlines, were arrested.

Sound Up Salomi Mckuur
Devi: How did you react when you found out that your brothers were charged under the terrorism act?

Salomi: We were shocked. If you know my brothers, what type of boys they are… We, my family is shocked. And we… ja, we are at a loss for words.

Voice
Brandon-Lee was arrested first last week Saturday when the Hawks raided the house he and his mother share in Newclare, Johannesburg at around 6 in the morning.

Sound Up Salomi
They were basically pulled out of bed, they were sleeping. They heard a loud bang on the door, they thought it was gunshots.

Voice
After searching the house and confiscating documents, the police arrested Brandon-Lee and told him to take them to Tony-Lee’s house.

Sound Up Salomi
They eventually came into my brothers cottage, where him and his wife were sleeping, they did the same, they were pointing the guns at them, and they asked my brother to get dressed and come to the living area.

Voice
Both men appeared briefly in the Johannesburg Magistrates Court this week and remain behind bars until their next court appearance this coming Tuesday.

Devi: Tell me about your brothers, what are they like?

Salomi: My brothers are the most kindest people that you’d ever meet. Just for an example, Brandon, he works for R8000 a month. He gives my mother seven of that R8000 every month. Without fail. That is the type of boy he his… The same for Tony, he is exactly the same. So Tony does not work, but he would give his last for whoever needed.

Voice
The family deny that Brandon and Tony–Lee have any links to terrorism.

Sound Up Salomi
Devi: It’s a straightforward question but I have to ask it. Do you believe your brothers are terrorists?

Salomi: No, no. Not at all.

Devi: Do you think your brothers are innocent and have been accused of something they didn’t do?
Salomi: Innocent until proven guilty.

Voice
The family also deny that the twins have any links to ISIS, even though they have attempted to move to Syria in the past. Family spokesperson Karen Jayes says the twins wanted to immigrate to Syria, not join ISIS.

Sound Up Karen
They did not go to Syria to fight for ISIS, they went to Syria to live under what they understood to be an Islamic government.

Voice
Karen, who works for Cage Africa, a non profit that fights for the rights of people accused of terrorism says reports that the twins were prevented from leaving SA by the police are incorrect.

Sound Up Karen
Their sister Salomi called the airline, it was not the police.

Voice
News of planned bombings against Jewish institutions have alarmed the Jewish Community in South Africa. Chief Rabbi Dr Warren Goldstein, who we spoke to via Skype, says this is an issue that should concern every single South African.

Sound Up Warren
The problem of radical Jihadi terror is one that affects human beings of civilized societies and nations all over the world, and their victims are christians, jews, muslims, hindus. We are talking here about a global problem of radical Jihadi terror.

Voice
Jasmin Opperman is the African Director of the Terrorism Research Analysis Consortium. She says the ISIS propaganda machine has rolled into South Africa.

Sound Up Jasmin
The fact that we have between 30 and 50 South Africans in the caliphate means that this propaganda that is being spread, is finding an audience, is finding people who are showing sympathy, showing loyalty. But not only loyalty, a willingness to act upon this loyalty.

Voice
Jasmin says South Africans who believe our relatively neutral position in world politics will protect us from an ISIS attack are naïve.

Sound Up Jasmin
The South African government cannot walk the tightrope anymore. If our president visits France, official visit, what is the message ISIS will see in it? The arrests have been made, what is the message ISIS reads in it?

Sound Up Salomi
Devi: Did you ask them that question, did you ask them if they did this? What did they say?

Salomi: They just said you know me. That’s all they said. And they ok, we shouldn’t worry. He’s worried about my mom. Both of them.

Devi: Experts have said to us that when people become radicalized there is an immediate change in behavior, they speak a different language. Did you pick up anything? Any changes?

Salomi: No. They are the same boys I grew up with. Nothing. And I was with them everyday. Nothing changed.

Voice
Secretary General of the Muslim Council of Theologens Moulana Ebrahim Bham says ISIS is a distortion of Islam.

Sound Up Ebrahim
Ebrahim: Islamic State is guilty of unambiguous and obvious violations of the Islamic law. And it stands, distorting the Islamic message. Now that has been the very clear-cut message which has come out of the United Ulema Council of South Africa.

Voice
Moulana Ebrahim says that mainstream Islam is fighting fire with fire by also employing platforms such as social media to reach the faithful.

Sound Up Ebrahim
Our organization has a dedicated channel, a BBM channel, a Whatsapp group in which it propagates its views and its ideals and its viewpoints. Personally myself I am on social media, I am on Twitter, and I have thousands of followers.

Voice
Karen says that the Thulsie brother’s case will set a precedent in South Africa, and hopes that the rule of law will prevail.

Sound Up Karen
Especially in the United States we know that 90% of the terrorism cases and arrests that have been made of individuals allegedly about to commit a terrorist attack have been made after they have been lured or entrapped

Voice
Salomi says her mother, Wasiela Thulsie, who was in the house when Brandon Lee was arrested, has been left traumatized by the way police treated her.

Sound Up Salomi
Devi: How old is your mom?

Salomi: 52

Devi: What was her state, how is she even doing now?

Salomi: She’s not doing very well. She’s not. She’s traumatized. Obviously first of all she’s worried about my brothers – her children. And second of all I think what happened and the manner in which it happened and how she was treated, she’s still not over that.

Sound Up Karen
There was a situation during the arrest where Wasiela Thulsie was made… The police officer pointed at the Quran, the holy Quran, and said read it. And she refused to read it and she refused to read it because of the situation and they started to laugh at her. And this kind of Islamaphobia and this kind of anti-Muslim bias creeping into the police behavior is very worrying to us.

Voice
We asked the Hawks for comment in this program but they declined to be interviewed.

Link Devi
Experts warn that a lack of transparency from the authorities could result in terror attacks on South African soil.

Sound Up Martin
The government need to be very cautious, because we have seen with other countries around the world, how the wrong response to terrorism could actually trigger more attacks. Could actually instead of killing the threat, could actually fuels the threat.

Sound Up Jasmin
The court case has to be transparent for the people of South Africa to know what the facts surrounding this case are.

Voice
Despite the serious charges against her brothers, Salomi remains convinced of their innocence.

Sound Up Salomi
Devi: What do you want South Africans to know about your brothers?

Salomi: They are good boys, they have good hearts. They are caring, they are loving, they wouldn’t harm a fly.
